nodes.name: Nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: \barr{ll} u_t-\Delta\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)u)=0\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rr^d),\vsp u(0,x)=u_0(x), \earr
nodes.statement_short: Nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation $u_t-\Delta\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)u)=0$ with initial datum $u_0$.
nodes.label: e1.1

nodes.name: Hypothesis (i): monotone $C^1$ diffusion $\beta$
nodes.statement: {\it$\beta(0)=0$, $\b\in C^1(\rr)$, and \begin{equation} \g_0|r_1-r_2|^2\le(\b(r_1)-\b(r_2))(r_1-r_2),\ r_1,r_2\in\rr, \end{equation} where $0<\g_0<\9.$ }
nodes.statement_short: $\beta$ is $C^1$, $\beta(0)=0$, and strongly monotone: $(\beta(r_1)-\beta(r_2))(r_1-r_2)\ge\gamma_0|r_1-r_2|^2$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii): bounded continuous drift $b$, locally Lipschitz in $r$
nodes.statement: $b\in C_b(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd)$, $b(x, \cdot) \in C^1(\rrd; \rrd)$ $ \forall x\in\rrd$ {\it such that} $$\mbox{$\sup\{|b^i_r(x,r)|;x\in\rrd,i=1,2,$ $|r|\le M\}\le C_M,$ $\ff M>0.$}$$
nodes.statement_short: $b$ is bounded continuous, $C^1$ in $r$, with $\sup_x|b^i_r(x,r)|\le C_M$ for $|r|\le M$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii'): $b(x,0)=0$, $b\in C^1$ with bounded $\delta(r)=\sup_x|b_x(x,r)|$
nodes.statement: $b(x,0)=0$ $\forall x\in\rrd$, $b \in C^1(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd) $ {\it and for $$\delta(r):=\sup\{|b_x(x,r)|;\ x\in\rrd\},$$we have} $\delta\in C_b(\rr).$
nodes.statement_short: $b(x,0)=0$, $b\in C^1(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ and $\delta(r)=\sup_x|b_x(x,r)|$ is bounded continuous.

nodes.name: Notation $b^i$, $b^i_r$, $b_x$
nodes.statement: $$b(x,u)=\{b^i(x,u)\}^d_{i=1}\mbox{ and }b^i_r=\frac{\pp b^i}{\pp r}, b_x=\big\{ \nabla_x \, b^i(x, \cdot) \big\}_{i=1}^d.$$

nodes.statement: In the following, we shall use the notation $b^*(x,u)=b(x,u)u.$

nodes.name: Existence of mild solutions to (1.1) (Barbu--R\"ockner [1])
nodes.statement: In \cite{1} it was proved, in particular, that, if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr,$ we have $\Phi\in C^2(\rr)$, then there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)--(ii) and $\Phi=\beta(u)/u\in C^2$, (1.1) has a mild solution $u\in C([0,\infty);L^1)$ for every $u_0\in L^1$.
conclusions: there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$

nodes.name: Mild solution
nodes.statement: The mild solution $u$ is defined~as $$u(t)=\lim_{h\to0}u_h(t)\mbox{ in }L^1(\rr^d),\ \ff t\ge0,$$where \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_h(t)=u^i_h\mbox{ for }t\in[ih,(i+h)h],\ i=0,1,...,Nh=T,\vsp u^{i+1}_h-h\D\b(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b(x,u^{i+1}_h)u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h\mbox{ in }\cald'(\rr^d),\\\hfill i=0,1,...,\vsp u^0_h=u_0.\earr \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The mild solution is the $L^1$-limit as $h\to0$ of the implicit time-discretization scheme (1.6).

nodes.name: Implicit time-discretization scheme (1.6) for the mild solution
nodes.statement: \barr{l} u_h(t)=u^i_h\mbox{ for }t\in[ih,(i+h)h],\ i=0,1,...,Nh=T,\vsp u^{i+1}_h-h\D\b(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b(x,u^{i+1}_h)u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h\mbox{ in }\cald'(\rr^d),\\\hfill i=0,1,...,\vsp u^0_h=u_0.\earr
nodes.statement_short: Implicit Euler scheme $u^{i+1}_h-h\Delta\beta(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h$ whose limit defines the mild solution.
nodes.label: e1.6

nodes.name: Nonexpansive semigroup $S(t)$ generated by the mild solution
nodes.statement: Moreover, $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$.
nodes.statement_short: The mild-solution map $S(t)u_0=u(t)$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of $L^1$-nonexpansive mappings.
assumptions: if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr,$ we have $\Phi\in C^2(\rr)$
conclusions: $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$

nodes.name: Mild solutions are distributional solutions
nodes.statement: As easily seen, any mild solution is a distributional solution but the uniqueness follows in the class of mild solutions only.
nodes.statement_short: Every mild solution is a distributional solution, but uniqueness was only known within the mild class.
conclusions: any mild solution is a distributional solution

nodes.name: McKean--Vlasov SDE (1.7)
nodes.statement: dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt+\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{\b(u(t,X(t))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t).
nodes.statement_short: McKean--Vlasov SDE whose diffusion coefficient depends on the law density $u$.
nodes.label: e1.7

nodes.name: Notation: function spaces $L^p$, $H^k$, $H^{-k}$, $C_b$, $C^k$, $C^1_b$
nodes.statement: Denote by $L^p(\rr^d)=L^p$ the space of $p$-summable functions on $L^p$, with the norm denoted $|\cdot|_p$. By $H^k(\rrd)=H^k$, $k=1,2$, and $H^{-k}(\rrd)=H^{-k},$ we denote the standard Sobolev spaces on $\rrd$ and by $C_b(\rrd)$ the space of continuous and bounded functions on $\rrd$. By $C^k(\rrd)$ we denote the space of continuously differentiable functions on $\rrd$ of order $k$, by $C^1_b(\rrd)$ the space $\left\{u\in C^1(\rrd);\frac{\pp u}{\pp y}\in C_b(\rrd),\ j=1,...,d\right\}.$ The spaces of continuous and differentiable functions on $(0,T)\times\rrd$ are denoted in a similar way and we shall simply write $$C^1_b(\rrd)=C^1_b,\ C^k(\rrd)=C^k,\ k=1,2.$$ The scalar product in $L^2$ is denoted $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2$ and by ${}_{H^{-1}}\!\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{H^1}$ the pairing between $H^1$ and $H^{-1}.$ Of course, on $L^2\times L^2$ this coincides with $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2.$
nodes.statement_short: Standard notation for Lebesgue, Sobolev, bounded-continuous and $C^k$ spaces on $\mathbb R^d$, the $L^2$ scalar product and the $H^{-1}$--$H^1$ pairing.

nodes.name: Scalar product and norm on $H^{-1}$
nodes.statement: The~scalar product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{-1}$ on $H\1$ is taken~as \begin{equation} \<u,v\>_{-1}=\<(I-\D)\1u,v\>_2,\ \ff u,v\in H\1 \end{equation}with the corresponding norm \begin{equation} |u|_{-1}=(\<u,u\>_{-1})^{\frac12},\ u\in H\1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\langle u,v\rangle_{-1}=\langle (I-\Delta)^{-1}u,v\rangle_2$ and $|u|_{-1}=\langle u,u\rangle_{-1}^{1/2}$ on $H^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Notation: Schwartz distributions, $W^{1,2}([0,T];\mathcal X)$, $z_r$, $z_x$
nodes.statement: By $\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)$ and $\cald'(\rrd)$ we denote the space of Schwartz distributions on $(0,\9)\times\rrd$ and $\rrd$, respectively. If $\calx$ is a Banach space, we denote by $W^{1,2}([0,T];\calx)$ the infinite dimensional Sobolev space $\{y\in L^2(0,T;\calx);$ $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;\calx)\}$, where $\frac d{dt}$ is taken in the sense of vectorial distributions. We also set, for each $z\in C^1(\rrd\times\rr)$, $$z_r(x,r)=\frac\pp{\pp r}\ z(x,r),\ \ z_x=\nabla_x z(x,r).$$ We shall denote the norms on $\rrd$ and $\rr$ by the same symbol $|\cdot|$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal D'$ denotes Schwartz distributions; $W^{1,2}([0,T];\mathcal X)$ is the vector-valued Sobolev space with $y,dy/dt\in L^2(0,T;\mathcal X)$; $z_r,z_x$ are partial derivatives.

nodes.name: Uniqueness for $u_t-\Delta\beta(u)=0$ (Brezis--Crandall)
nodes.statement: In the special case $b\equiv0$, such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1} was established earlier in \cite{3} for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions $\b$.
nodes.statement_short: For $b\equiv0$ and continuous nondecreasing $\beta$, distributional solutions of (1.1) are unique.
assumptions: for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions $\b$
conclusions: such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1} was established

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 (uniqueness of distributional solutions)
nodes.statement: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold. For each $u_0\in L^\9\cap L^1$, the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)--(ii), for $u_0\in L^\infty\cap L^1$ the Fokker--Planck equation (1.1) has at most one distributional solution in $L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$.
assumptions: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold.
conclusions: the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
nodes.label: t1

nodes.name: Solution class $L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\infty$ (add-e5)
nodes.statement: u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).
nodes.label: add-e5

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd)$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr \end{equation} (Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \ff x\in\rrd,\ r\in\rr.$) It should be mentioned that, by (i), (ii), it follows that $u_i,\beta(u_i), b^*(\cdot, u_i)\in L^2((0,T);L^2),$ $i=1,2$, and, therefore, $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2}).$ Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$ Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1}, we have \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr \end{equation} where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$ (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.) Assume first that, in addition, \begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}). \end{equation} Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2} with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that $$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that $$\barr{l} \dd\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2 =\<\Gamma(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vsp \qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$ \begin{equation} \barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_2 \le\<\b(u_1(t))-\b(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vsp \qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\earr \end{equation} We note that \begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2. \end{equation} We also have \begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \ff F\in (L^2)^d. \end{equation}This yields \begin{equation} \barr{ll} |\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}| \le|\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)|_{2}|u|_{-1} \le\b_M|u|_2|u|_{-1} \earr\end{equation}and \begin{equation} \barr{l} \left|\<{\rm div}\ (b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}\right|\vsp \qquad\le 2|b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)|_2|u_1-u_2|_{-1}\vsp \qquad\le2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)|u|_2|u|_{-1}, \earr \end{equation} where $M=\max\{|u_1|_\9,|u_2|_\9)$ and $$\barr{lcl} \b_M&=&\dd\sup\{\b'(r);\ |r|\le M\},\vsp b_M&=&\dd\sup\left\{\frac{|b(x,u_1)-b(x,u_2)|}{|r_1-r_2|};\ x\in\rrd,\ |r_1|,|r_2|<M\right\}\vsp&\le& \sup\{|b_r(x,r)|;|r|\le M,\ x\in\rrd\} < \infty \earr$$ by (ii). By \eqref{e2.3}--\eqref{e2.7}, we get $$\barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_{2} \le(\b_M+2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9) |u(t)|^{}_2|u(t)|^{}_{-1},\\\hfill\mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ This yields $$\frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}\le C|u(t)|^2_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).$$Since $u:[0,T]\to H^{-1}$ is absolutely continuous and narrowly continuous, we infer that $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, $\ff t\in[0,T]$, and so $u\equiv0$, as claimed. To conclude the proof, we shall prove
nodes.statement_short: $H^{-1}$ energy estimate: set $u=u_1-u_2$, test (2.2) with $u$, use monotonicity (1.2) and bounds (2.4)--(2.7) to get $\frac d{dt}|u|^2_{-1}\le C|u|^2_{-1}$, hence $u\equiv0$; the needed regularity (add-e6) is supplied by Claim 2.2.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: By It\^o's formula, both $u$ and $\wt u$ satisfy the (nonlinear) \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} in the sense of Schwartz distributions. Hence, by Theorem \ref{t1}, $u=\wt u$. Furthermore, again by It\^o's formula, $\mathbb{P}\circ X\1$ and $\mathbb{P}\circ\wt X\1$ satisfy the martingale problem with the initial condition $u_0dx$ for the linear Komogorov operator $$L_u:=\Phi(u)\D+b(\cdot,u)\cdot\nabla,$$where $\Phi(u)=\frac{\b(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr.$ Hence, by Theorem \ref{t5}, the assertion follows by Lemma 2.12 in \cite{4}. Here, for $s\in[0,T]$, the set $\mathcal{R}_{[s,T]}$, which appears in that lemma, is chosen to be the set of all narrowly continuous, probability measure-valued solutions of \eqref{e3.1} having for each $t\in[s,T]$ a density \mbox{$v(t,\cdot)\in L^\9$} with respect to Lebesgue measure such that \mbox{$v\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$}

nodes.name: Set $u=u_1-u_2$ and write its equation (2.1)
nodes.statement: Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd)$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr \end{equation} (Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \ff x\in\rrd,\ r\in\rr.$)
nodes.statement_short: Introduce two solutions, their difference $u$, and the equation (2.1) it satisfies.

nodes.name: Regularity of $u_i$ and $u$ from (i), (ii)
nodes.statement: It should be mentioned that, by (i), (ii), it follows that $u_i,\beta(u_i), b^*(\cdot, u_i)\in L^2((0,T);L^2),$ $i=1,2$, and, therefore, $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2}).$
nodes.statement_short: Hypotheses give $u_i,\beta(u_i),b^*(\cdot,u_i)\in L^2(L^2)$ and $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2})$.

nodes.name: Introduce $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}$, $y=\Gamma u$ and derive (2.2)
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$ Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1}, we have \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr \end{equation} where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$ (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.)
nodes.statement_short: Apply the isomorphism $\Gamma$ to (2.1) to get the $L^2$-valued equation (2.2) for $y=\Gamma u$.

nodes.name: Assume extra regularity (add-e6)
nodes.statement: Assume first that, in addition, \begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Temporarily assume $u\in L^2(0,T;H^1)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1})$ (justified later by Claim 2.2).

nodes.name: Test (2.2) with $u$
nodes.statement: Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2} with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that $$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that $$\barr{l} \dd\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2 =\<\Gamma(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vsp \qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$
nodes.statement_short: Take the $L^2$ scalar product of (2.2) with $u$ and use $\langle u_t,u\rangle_{-1}=\frac12\frac d{dt}|u|^2_{-1}$.

nodes.name: Apply monotonicity (1.2) to get (2.3)
nodes.statement: By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$ \begin{equation} \barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_2 \le\<\b(u_1(t))-\b(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vsp \qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\earr \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Strong monotonicity of $\beta$ yields the coercive energy inequality (2.3).

nodes.name: Recall bounds (2.4), (2.5)
nodes.statement: We note that \begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2. \end{equation} We also have \begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \ff F\in (L^2)^d. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Record $|\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2$ and $|{\rm div}F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2$.

nodes.name: Bound the right-hand side: (2.6), (2.7)
nodes.statement: This yields \begin{equation} \barr{ll} |\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}| \le|\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)|_{2}|u|_{-1} \le\b_M|u|_2|u|_{-1} \earr\end{equation}and \begin{equation} \barr{l} \left|\<{\rm div}\ (b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}\right|\vsp \qquad\le 2|b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)|_2|u_1-u_2|_{-1}\vsp \qquad\le2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)|u|_2|u|_{-1}, \earr \end{equation} where $M=\max\{|u_1|_\9,|u_2|_\9)$ and $$\barr{lcl} \b_M&=&\dd\sup\{\b'(r);\ |r|\le M\},\vsp b_M&=&\dd\sup\left\{\frac{|b(x,u_1)-b(x,u_2)|}{|r_1-r_2|};\ x\in\rrd,\ |r_1|,|r_2|<M\right\}\vsp&\le& \sup\{|b_r(x,r)|;|r|\le M,\ x\in\rrd\} < \infty \earr$$ by (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Estimate both right-hand terms of (2.3) by $C|u|_2|u|_{-1}$ using local Lipschitz constants $\beta_M,b_M$ from (ii).

nodes.name: Combine into a differential inequality for $|u|^2_{-1}$
nodes.statement: By \eqref{e2.3}--\eqref{e2.7}, we get $$\barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_{2} \le(\b_M+2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9) |u(t)|^{}_2|u(t)|^{}_{-1},\\\hfill\mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ This yields $$\frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}\le C|u(t)|^2_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).$$
nodes.statement_short: Absorb $|u|_2|u|_{-1}$ with the coercive term to get $\frac d{dt}|u|^2_{-1}\le C|u|^2_{-1}$.

nodes.name: Conclude $u\equiv0$; reduce to Claim 2.2
nodes.statement: Since $u:[0,T]\to H^{-1}$ is absolutely continuous and narrowly continuous, we infer that $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, $\ff t\in[0,T]$, and so $u\equiv0$, as claimed. To conclude the proof, we shall prove
nodes.statement_short: Gronwall with $u(0)=0$ gives $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, so $u\equiv0$; it remains to prove the assumed regularity (Claim 2.2).

nodes.name: Rewrite (1.1) around $|u_0|_\infty+\alpha(t)$

nodes.name: Construct $\alpha$ via the ODE (2.11)
nodes.statement: We may find $\a$ of the form $\a=\eta-|u_0|_\9,$ where $\eta$ is a solution to the equation \begin{equation} \barr{l} \eta'-\delta(\eta)\eta =0,\ t\ge0,\vsp \eta(0)=|u_0|_\9,\earr \end{equation} $\delta(r)=\sup\{|b_x(x,r)|;x\in\rrd\},$ $r\in\rr.$ Clearly, \eqref{e2.11} has such a solution $\eta\in C^1([0,\9)),$ $\eta\ge0,$ on $[0,\9)$ because $\delta\in C_b(\rr).$
nodes.statement_short: Take $\alpha=\eta-|u_0|_\infty$ with $\eta'=\delta(\eta)\eta$, $\eta(0)=|u_0|_\infty$, solvable since $\delta\in C_b$ by (ii').

nodes.name: Formal comparison argument
nodes.statement: Formally, if we multiply \eqref{e2.9} by ${\rm sign}(u-|u_0|_\9-\a)^+$, integrate over $\rrd$ and use the monotonicity of $\b$, we get by \eqref{e2.5} that \begin{equation} \frac d{dt}\,|(u(t)-|u_0|_\9-\a(t))^+|_1\le0,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T). \end{equation}This yields $u(t)\le|u_0|_\9+\a(t)$, $\ff t\ge0$, and similarly it follows that $u(t)\ge-|u_0|_\9-\a(t).$ Hence, $u\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd),$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Formally testing (2.9) with ${\rm sign}(u-|u_0|_\infty-\alpha)^+$ gives (2.11a), hence $|u|\le|u_0|_\infty+\alpha(t)$ and $u\in L^\infty$.

nodes.statement: Then, as proved earlier in \cite{1}, \cite{2az}, \cite{2}, equation \eqref{e2.11aaa} has a unique solution $u_\vp\in L^2(0,T;H^1)\cap C([0,T];L^1)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];H\1)$ and $u_\vp\to u$ in $C([0,T];L^1)$ as $\vp\to0$. An easy way to prove this is to apply the Trotter--Kato theorem to the family of $m$-accretive operators in $L^1$ $$\barr{lcl} A_\vp u&=&-\D\b(u)+\vp\b(u)+{\rm div}(b_\vp(x,u)u),\vsp D(A_\vp)&=&\{u\in L^1;-\Delta\beta(u)+\vp\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b_\vp(x,u)u)\in L^1\}.\earr$$ (See the argument in \cite{2}.)
nodes.statement_short: By [1], [2az], [2] (or Trotter--Kato for the $m$-accretive $A_\varepsilon$), (2.11aaa) has a unique regular solution $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in $C([0,T];L^1)$.

nodes.statement: Then, we replace \eqref{e2.9} by \begin{equation} \barr{l} (u_\vp-|u_0|_\9-\a(t))_t-\D(\b(u_\vp)-\b(|u_0|_\9+\a(t)))\vsp +\vp(\b(u)-\b(|u_0|_\9+\a(t)))+{\rm div}(b^*_\vp(x,u_\vp)-b^*_\vp(x,|u_0|_\9+\a(t))\vsp =-b^*_\vp(x,|u_0|_\9+\a(t))-\a'(t)-\vp\beta(|u_0|_\9+\a(t))\le0,\vsp\hfill \mbox{ a.e. in }(0,T)\times\rrd,\earr\end{equation} where $b^*_\vp(u)=b_\vp(u)u.$

nodes.name: Let $\delta\to0$: $u_\varepsilon\le|u_0|_\infty+\alpha$
nodes.statement: Then, by \eqref{e2.11aa}, we get, for $\delta\to0$, $$\int_\rrd(u_\vp-|u_0|_\9-\a(t))^+_t\,dx\le0,\ \ff t\in(0,T),$$and this yields $$u_\vp(t,x)-|u_0|_\9-\a(t)\le0,\mbox{ a.e. on }(0,T)\times\rrd,$$and so, $u_\vp\le|u_0|_\9+\a$, a.e. on $(0,T)\times\rrd$.

nodes.statement: Then, we pass to the limit $\vp\to0$ to get the claimed inequality.

nodes.name: Set $v=v_1-v_2$; assume regularity (add-e6)
nodes.statement: We shall proceed as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}. Namely, we set $v_1-v_2=v$ for two solutions $v_1,v_2$ of \eqref{e3.2} By a similar argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}, we may assume that $v$ satisfies \eqref{add-e6}.

nodes.name: Equation (3.3) for $v$
nodes.statement: Then we get \begin{equation} \barr{l} v_t-\D(\Psi v)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)v)=0,\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\vsp v(0)=0.\earr \end{equation}

nodes.name: Apply $\Gamma$ and test with $v$: energy inequality (3.5)
nodes.statement: For $y=\Gamma v$, we get \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac d{dt}\ y-\Gamma\D(\Psi v)+\Gamma\ {\rm div}(b(x,u)v)=0\vsp y(0)=0\earr \end{equation} and multiplying scalarly in $L^2$ with $v$, as above we get that \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\ |v(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|v(t)|^2_2 \le(|\Psi|_\9+|b|_\9)|v(t)|^{}_2|v(t)|^{}_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\Gamma$ to get (3.4), multiply by $v$ in $L^2$ as before, obtaining (3.5) with coercive term $\gamma_0|v|^2_2$.

nodes.name: Conclude $v\equiv0$
nodes.statement: This yields $$\frac d{dt}\ |v(t)|^2_{-1}\le|v(t)|^2_{-1}\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$ and, therefore, $v\equiv0$, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Absorb to get $\frac d{dt}|v|^2_{-1}\le|v|^2_{-1}$ and conclude $v\equiv0$ by Gronwall.

nodes.name: Conclude via Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 2.12 of [4]
nodes.statement: Hence, by Theorem \ref{t5}, the assertion follows by Lemma 2.12 in \cite{4}. Here, for $s\in[0,T]$, the set $\mathcal{R}_{[s,T]}$, which appears in that lemma, is chosen to be the set of all narrowly continuous, probability measure-valued solutions of \eqref{e3.1} having for each $t\in[s,T]$ a density \mbox{$v(t,\cdot)\in L^\9$} with respect to Lebesgue measure such that \mbox{$v\in L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).$}
